statement: Steady-state error is the discrepancy between the desired target value (setpoint or reference, denoted $\text{SP}$) and the actual value of the system (process variable, denoted $\text{PV}$) as the control system drives the system toward its desired state, characterized by the error value equation $e = \text{SP} - \text{PV}$.

symbols.meaning: error value or error signal representing the difference between desired and actual system values
setpoint or reference value representing the desired target state of the system
process variable representing the actual measured value of the system under control
control signal or manipulated variable output by the controller to actuate the system

properties.property: Inclusion of an integrator in the open-loop chain directly before the system under control achieves rejection of a step disturbance.
properties.why: integral action accumulates the persistent error signal over time to provide corrective input until the error is eliminated

properties.property: Minimizing steady-state error is a primary control objective evaluated alongside delay, peak overshoot, and system stability.
properties.why: feedback controllers are synthesized to drive the process variable to the setpoint while maintaining closed-loop stability and transient performance

properties.property: The error signal provides the corrective feedback driving proportional, integral, and derivative control terms.
properties.why: the controller continuously monitors the difference between the setpoint and process variable to compute the corrective control action $u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau + K_d \frac{\mathrm{d}e(t)}{\mathrm{d}t} + u_0$

assumptions.assumption: All bad or unstable dynamics of the system states are both controllable and observable (or stabilizable and detectable).
assumptions.breaks_when: An unstable eigenvalue is uncontrollable or unobservable, causing uncontrollable unstable dynamics to persist in the closed-loop system.

assumptions.assumption: The closed-loop control system is BIBO stable with all poles located strictly in the stability region (e.g., inside the unit circle $|z| < 1$ for discrete-time systems or $\mathrm{Re}[\lambda] < 0$ for continuous-time systems).
assumptions.breaks_when: Improper controller tuning or pole placement positions closed-loop poles on or outside the stability boundary (e.g., $|z| \ge 1$ or $\mathrm{Re}[\lambda] \ge 0$).

assumptions.assumption: The control signal and physical actuators operate within their allowable linear operating thresholds without saturation.
assumptions.breaks_when: Control demands exceed physical limits (such as actuator travel limits or valve slew rates), causing degraded tracking, actuator damage, or integrator windup without anti-windup protection.

failure_modes.signature: System output and error signal grow unboundedly (e.g., exponential divergence $x[n] = 1.5^n u[n]$).
failure_modes.cause: A pole of the closed-loop transfer function has modulus strictly greater than one ($|z| > 1$) or a positive real part.

failure_modes.mode: Actuator damage or tracking failure from physical constraints
failure_modes.signature: Controller requests control signals exceeding actuator rate or magnitude limits, leading to saturation or mechanical breakdown.
failure_modes.cause: Neglecting physical input and state constraints during controller synthesis without implementing anti-windup or constraint-handling systems.

failure_modes.mode: Derivative spike response on step setpoint change
failure_modes.signature: Severe, sudden spikes in the control signal $u(t)$ immediately following abrupt changes in the reference setpoint.
failure_modes.cause: Direct differentiation of a step discontinuity in the error signal $e(t)$ via the $K_d \frac{\mathrm{d}e(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}$ term without low-pass filtering.
